_comment: exec_shape golden fixture (§1.1). AUTHORED, not generated: it pins intended semantics, so a regenerated version would assert nothing. Python derives the shape; the plugin does not, but must agree on heads/parse_ok for localAllowlist. Only the keys present in `expect` are asserted, so a case can pin one field without restating the rest.
Wrappers. Both of the next two were bugs in the first implementation: a flag-skipping loop alone yields heads of `30` and `root`.
inline_eval — the flag decides, not the head. `python3 script.py` is not inline eval; `python3 -c` is.
Sinks, classified by the head of the stage being fed into.

The next four are the single highest-value cases in this file. A naive `any file_redirect is a sink` rule fired on 52% of corpus commands — every sampled one being `2>/dev/null` or `2>&1`. Since every allow rule requires sinks to be empty, that would have made half of all traffic permanently allow-ineligible: most of Phase 3b's relief, gone, with every test still green. Fixing it moved sink-free from 48% to 96% of the corpus.
Redaction. F11/F16: the post-1A wire format stays parseable, including markers and preserved provider prefixes. These are the cases that let Phase 3b trust `parse_ok` on real traffic.

F12: the historical binary-name redaction. Current sanitize cannot produce this (D14 head guard), but 58 corpus rows carry it. tree-sitter parses `[REDACTED]` as a test_command, strands the `-` in an ERROR node, and reads `c` as a genuine command_name of a following command — so the head is correctly extracted from an incorrectly parsed command, and no token-level check can catch it. What must hold is that the damage is *declared*: parse_ok false and no segments. CONSEQUENCE FOR PHASE 3B: any heads distribution must filter on parse_ok, or it inherits exactly the `c` / `get` / `help` junk seen in the corpus histogram.
Packing. A packed excerpt can parse *successfully* into misleading heads, which is worse than failing — so packing is detected before the parser runs and forces parse_ok=false with no heads at all.
Fail closed: segments are dropped when the parse is not clean, so no allow rule can build a constraint on a structure we do not trust. Heads survive for diagnostics.

Privilege elevation. Stripping sudo is correct for detection rules (a rule hunting `exec:cat` must still see it) but makes elevation invisible to `heads`, which is the field Phase 3b allow rules key on: `cat /etc/passwd` and `sudo cat /etc/shadow` have identical heads. Two shipping agent tools get this wrong — crush prefix-matches `timeout rm -rf /` as safe, and Codex strips sudo with a blind argv[1..] so `sudo -u root rm -rf /` becomes `-u root rm -rf /`. `privileged` exists so an allow rule can refuse elevation with one constraint, enforced at compile time in 1B-3 rather than left to rule authors to remember.
